title: Bechukotai: still remembered (Leviticus 26:42–45)
hook: even after the warnings, God remembers the covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tochacha, the warnings read in a low voice. Your line was hard words, softly. Today, the end of that chapter.

There's a drawer in a lot of homes with old things nobody throws out: a hospital bracelet from a birth, a note in a grandparent's handwriting, a ring that doesn't fit anyone anymore. The things in that drawer have outlived the quarrels around them. A family can fight for years, and the drawer still holds the proof that someone once promised to love someone. The warnings in Leviticus twenty-six get very dark: an empty land, a scattered people. Then, right at the bottom, the chapter opens a drawer.
screen: `A DRAWER OF OLD PROMISES.` → `IT OUTLIVES THE QUARRELS.` → `AT THE BOTTOM, A DRAWER OPENS.`

segments.voice: Verse forty-two. After the exile, after the empty fields, God says: "then will I remember My covenant with Jacob, and also My covenant with Isaac, and also My covenant with Abraham will I remember; and I will remember the land." Listen to the order. Not Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the way the names usually run. It goes backwards. Rashi offers a reading: it's as if God reaches back one generation at a time. Jacob alone would be reason enough; and if not, there's Isaac with him; and if not, Abraham. The memory keeps reaching further back until it finds enough. Verse forty-four says what remembering means in practice. Even when they're in the land of their enemies, God will not reject them, nor abhor them so as to destroy them utterly, and break the covenant. And verse forty-five adds one more memory: the covenant with the generation brought out of Egypt. Notice what the chapter doesn't do. It doesn't cancel the warnings or pretend they weren't said. The hard words stand. But the chapter closes on memory, a promise older than the failure, held by the one who made it. The relationship can be strained to breaking. Verse forty-four says it isn't broken.
screen: `THEN WILL I REMEMBER.` · `BACKWARDS: JACOB, ISAAC, ABRAHAM.` · `NOT REJECTED, NOT ABHORRED.` · `THE WARNINGS STAND. MEMORY ENDS IT.` · then, large: `STILL REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Go back through the years slowly, the way the verse goes back through the generations, and find one promise once made to you: a parent who said I'll always come get you, a teacher who said you can do this, a friend who said call me, any hour. Remember the voice, the room, the moment. Notice that the promise still exists, even if the person is far away, or gone, or changed.
Bechukotai, Leviticus's last portion. After the blessings and the warnings, it ends with God remembering: the covenant, the ancestors, and the land.
Your line: still remembered. The warnings stand, and the promise is older. Day four hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: When the warnings of Leviticus 26 are read in many synagogues, the reader's voice returns to full strength for the closing verses of remembrance; the theme of God remembering the covenant with the ancestors runs through Jewish prayer, especially on Rosh Hashanah.

chat.says: After all those curses, does Leviticus 26 end with God giving up on the people?
options: No. It ends with God remembering the covenant: not rejected, not abhorred.
Yes. The warnings cancel the covenant until the people earn it back.
No, because it takes the warnings back and says they never applied.
chat.meaning: Verses 42 to 45: God remembers the covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham and won't reject them. The warnings stand, but memory ends the chapter.
